strengths: Rigorous and complete theoretical development: e-value/supermartingale constructions, Ville's inequality-based FWER control, Kelly-optimal betting analysis, mixture martingales for unknown deviation magnitude, and e-BH-based FDR control are all proven carefully, with full proofs deferred to a very thorough appendix.

Clear, well-motivated improvements over the closest prior work (Babichenko et al., 2017): the method is sequential/anytime rather than requiring a fixed sample size, does not require knowledge of the equilibrium strategy itself (only counterfactual payoffs), and yields sharper (linear rather than super-exponential) bounds for correlated equilibrium testing.

Nice unification across equilibrium concepts (Nash, correlated, coarse correlated, approximate) and a genuine extension from static normal-form games to stochastic games via a likelihood-ratio SPRT-type construction, including KL-divergence-based detection-time bounds and an ergodicity-based analysis.

The FDR extension via e-BH is a valuable practical contribution for large games, with a clean theoretical guarantee (Theorem 2.8) and a provable ordering result (Proposition 2.9) showing FDR control is never slower than FWER control.

Experiments are reasonably comprehensive: they empirically validate FWER control, demonstrate FDR speedup with sample-level scatter plots, verify the predicted O(1/ε²) scaling law in a stochastic game, and test robustness to unknown deviation magnitude via the mixture approach; a larger-scale (n=20, m=60 hypotheses) population game experiment in the appendix supports scalability of the qualitative findings.

Honest treatment of limitations (counterfactual payoff access, requiring knowledge of target policy in stochastic games) and inclusion of a concrete counterexample (Appendix E) justifying the necessity of the slack parameter η.
weaknesses: The core statistical toolkit (e-values, coin-betting constructions, Ville's inequality, mixture martingales, e-BH for FDR) is largely adapted from existing sequential testing / safe anytime-valid inference literature (Waudby-Smith & Ramdas, Wang & Ramdas, Robbins, etc.); the paper's novelty lies primarily in the application to game-theoretic equilibrium monitoring rather than in fundamentally new statistical machinery, which somewhat limits the technical originality relative to the statistics literature it builds on.

There is a conceptual tension between the paper's motivating narrative (learning agents whose behavior gradually or abruptly drifts away from equilibrium over time due to updating objectives/adapting strategies) and the actual technical model, which assumes the joint action profile is drawn i.i.d. from a *fixed* (possibly unknown) distribution at every round under both H0 and H1; this does not naturally capture continuously evolving/non-stationary learning dynamics, and the paper does not clearly reconcile this gap.

The requirement of observing counterfactual payoff evaluations ui(a'_i, a_-i) for every possible deviation in the normal-form setting, and of knowing the target policy π in the stochastic-game setting, are significant practical restrictions; while acknowledged as limitations and future work, no concrete methodology (e.g., value-function estimation) is offered to bridge this gap, limiting immediate real-world applicability.

All experiments are on synthetic, relatively small or moderate-scale simulated environments (2×2 games, 5×4 grid soccer, 10×10 predator-prey, a 20-player RPS population game); there is no real-world or naturally occurring multi-agent dataset used to validate the framework's practical utility, e.g., in economic, trading, or LLM-agent settings mentioned as motivating applications.

The data-splitting/screening baseline introduced in Appendix H.2 to reduce multiple-testing burden is argued informally (via independence of screening/testing windows) rather than being fully integrated into the paper's formal theoretical framework, leaving a slight gap between the appendix experiments and the core theory.

Presentation is extremely dense, with substantial material (including most novel technical content beyond Section 2's core results) relegated to a very long appendix; the main text alone may leave readers without a full picture of the contribution's scope and rigor.
